# `hostile_strings` — set README

Hand-authored per [[adrs/ADR-0131-extract-python-code-docs-with-griffe-and-scope-dis]]
clause 10: "Every target-derived string on a Python page or in a Python page's index
entry renders in a fence sized for it or escaped for its context, with line breaks and
control characters outside a fence rendered as visible escapes and link destinations
percent-encoded, so no target byte opens or closes page structure." This set is data
only; nothing here imports or runs Griffe, and no page was generated by a program.

## Manifest configuration a test must use

`{"extractor": "python", "include_private": true, "glob": ["**/*.py"]}`, run with
`src/` as the fixture's repository root, against the one scenario `expected/all-included/`.

## Sources and what each exercises

| Source | Exercises |
|---|---|
| `src/h1_backtick_runs.py` | A backtick run in a module docstring, an annotation string (a `Literal[...]` subscript, so the string is a real expression `ast.unparse` can round-trip — a bare forward-ref string annotation cannot hold arbitrary text, see decision D1 below), a default value, and an `__all__` entry. All four use a run of four backticks, so every fence/span in this page is sized to 5, distinctly proving R1/R5's `longest run + 1` formula rather than the coincidental default of 3. |
| `src/h2_link_and_comment_syntax.py` | The sequences `](` and `-->`/`<!--` in the same four contexts as the backtick-run file, proving each renders inert where it already sits inside a fence or a code span, needing no extra escaping there (R4 only escapes for the H1/index context, exercised separately by the file-name case below). |
| `src/h3_terminal_escapes.py` | A raw terminal escape byte (ESC, `0x1B`) in a module docstring (verbatim inside its R1 fence, per the dev-lead's ruling), and in an `__all__` entry and a default value, both of which reach R3's visible-escape spelling (`\x1b`) — the `__all__` entry via R5 (R3 applied before the code-span wrap), the default value via `ast.unparse`'s own `repr()`, which already escapes control bytes to the identical `\xNN` text R3 defines (see decision D2). |
| `` src/link](target)#frag.py `` | A committed file name carrying `]`, `(`, `)` and `#` (item 5 of the assignment). `]` and `#` are R4-escaped in the H1 and index title; `(` and `)` are not (R4 does not list them), which is safe once `]` is escaped, since `\]` can no longer close a link-text span. The index destination is percent-encoded per R6. |
| `src/h4_pep723_block.py` | A PEP 723 `# /// script` block (DL-3, 2026-09-25, dev-lead) whose TOML content carries a four-backtick run and `-->` inside a native TOML `#` comment line, proving `## Script metadata`'s fence sizes to the content (R1) rather than a fixed width, and that a TOML-level comment renders verbatim like any other fenced text. |
| `src/h5_line_break.py` | A line break (DL-5, 2026-09-25, dev-lead) inside an `__all__` string and inside a string default value. The `__all__` entry reaches R3's visible escape (`\n`) twice: once in the `## Exports` name-list code span, and once in the unresolved-export gap bullet, since no identifier can bind a name containing a newline. The default value stays inside the member's signature fence and renders through `ast.unparse`'s own escaping, which spells the same control character the identical way R3 does, so no second escaping path is invented for it. |
| `expected/hostile-names/cases.json` | Three file names that cannot be committed as real paths: a line break, a carriage return, and a terminal escape sequence — per the top README's "Stub-name and hostile-name fixtures that cannot be committed as files" section. |

Every `__all__` entry above whose string contains a backtick run or a hazardous
sequence has no corresponding real binding (no valid Python identifier can carry a
backtick, `]`, or an ESC byte), so each renders as an **unresolved export** gap per
clause 11 in addition to appearing in the `## Exports` name list. This is a
necessary, not incidental, consequence of testing a hostile `__all__` entry, so
each affected page carries one `## Exports` gap bullet, hand-verified against the
top README's gap-note grammar and R5 sizing.

## ADR-silent decisions (set-level)

**D1. An "annotation string" hazard uses a `Literal[...]` subscript, not a bare
forward-ref string.** R7 states a string-literal annotation renders as
`ast.unparse` of the *expression the string's content contains* — meaning a bare
forward-ref annotation (`x: "some text"`) must itself parse as a Python expression.
Arbitrary hostile text (a backtick run, `](`, `<!--`) is not valid Python syntax and
would raise `SyntaxError` if used this way. `Literal["hostile text"]` is a normal
subscript expression whose string argument imposes no such constraint, so it is
used here as the annotation-string hazard site. Rationale: this is the only
annotation shape in the ADR's page contract that can carry arbitrary hostile text
without producing an unparseable source file.

**D2. A hazardous default value is shown reaching the same visible-escape text as
R3, not additionally re-escaped.** The assignment's phrasing groups "an `__all__`
entry and a string default" under "outside a fence: visible escapes per R3". A
default value's signature always renders inside the member's signature fence per
clause 10 and R7 (verbatim, no further escaping) — so a default value is never
literally "outside a fence." What this set verifies instead: `ast.unparse`'s own
`repr()`-based escaping of a control byte (e.g. ESC becomes the four characters
`\x1b`) already produces the identical textual spelling R3 defines for the same
byte, so the fence-verbatim path and the outside-a-fence R3 path converge on the
same bytes for every control character R3 names (`\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\xNN`). This
fixture shows that convergence directly (`h3_terminal_escapes.py`'s default value
and `__all__` entry render identically once written out) rather than inventing a
second, contradictory rendering path for defaults.

**D3. `](`/`-->`/`<!--` are exercised in all four backtick-run contexts, not only a
docstring.** The assignment names these sequences without the explicit four-context
parenthetical it gives backtick runs, but "each case exercised in each context
where it can occur" reads most consistently applied uniformly across the two
structural-sequence cases. `h2_link_and_comment_syntax.py` mirrors
`h1_backtick_runs.py`'s shape for this reason.

**D4. `cases.json`'s `expected_h1`/`expected_index_line` values were computed
directly from R3/R4, not copied from the top README's illustrative example.**
The top README's worked example (`weird\\nname.py` case) doubled the backslash
count in `expected_h1` relative to what R3 alone produces for one line break (its
source escaped spelling used one backslash; its `expected_h1` used two). Applying
R4-then-R3 by hand and by a throwaway script (both cross-checked, see the report)
to the *same* raw path yields one backslash in `expected_h1`, matching the source
escaping exactly except for the `# ` prefix. This set's `cases.json` uses the
directly-computed values; the discrepancy was flagged for the dev-lead rather than
silently resolved, since the top README was out of this unit's ownership. DL-7
(2026-09-25) corrects the top README's illustration to match this set's committed
`cases.json`, so the two now agree.

**D5. `cases.json` destinations use the `python/` prefix, not `hostile_strings/`.**
This set's own manifest configuration (like every other set in this tree) writes
Python pages under `python/<path>.md`. The `python/` prefix is used here for
consistency with every other committed page in this tree and in this set's own
`expected/all-included/` pages. DL-7 (2026-09-25) also corrects the top README's
illustrative example, which had written the destination under a
`hostile_strings/` prefix, to the same `python/` prefix.

## What this file does not cover

No `--lang` scoping, no `--dry-run` byte comparison, no dispatcher or renderer code,
no test module. Per the top README, this tree's `real`/`private-excluded` scenario
already covers `include_private: false` exclusion generically, so no
`include_private: false` scenario is duplicated here.
